name: Portuguese colonization of Brazil
summary: Portugal claimed and settled Brazil, which would become the largest Portuguese-speaking nation and the mainstay of the colonial empire.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Brazil was initially neglected — the [spice trade](event:da-gama) was the prize — but sugar plantations and slave labour eventually made it immensely profitable. By 1800 Brazil was the empire's most valuable possession, and hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans had been landed there.

The colony developed its own identity, mixing Portuguese, indigenous and African peoples in ways the mainland did not, setting the stage for its independence in 1822.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Brazil).

name: Swahili city-states and Indian Ocean trade
summary: East African merchant cities from Mogadishu to Kilwa traded gold, ivory, and spices across the Indian Ocean, blending African and Arab cultures.
body:
The Swahili coast was not a European outpost but a sophisticated merchant civilization with its own ships, cities and rulers. Portuguese arrived in the 1500s and tried to monopolise the trade, but Arab, Persian and Indian merchants persisted, and the culture remained fundamentally African.

Swahili, still widely spoken today, is a Bantu language carrying heavy Arabic and Persian borrowing — the linguistic trace of centuries of Indian Ocean commerce.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_city-states).

name: Safavid Empire at its height
summary: Persia under the Safavids became a Shia Islamic empire, a great power rival to the Ottoman and Mughal empires.
body:
From Isfahan to the Caspian, Persian culture flourished — carpets, calligraphy, poetry, and architecture of extraordinary beauty. The Safavids made Shia Islam the state religion, a choice that shaped Iran's identity to this day.

Caught between Ottoman, Russian and Mughal powers, Safavid Persia ultimately fell to internal strife and external pressure, but its cultural inheritance remains one of history's glories.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Empire).

name: Leonardo paints the Mona Lisa
summary: Leonardo da Vinci's portrait became the most famous painting in the world.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). Leonardo da Vinci's portrait became the most famous painting in the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona_Lisa).

name: Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel
summary: Four years of work on scaffolding produced the ceiling frescoes of the Vatican chapel.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). Four years of work on scaffolding produced the ceiling frescoes of the Vatican chapel.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistine_Chapel_ceiling).

name: Portuguese conquest of Goa
summary: Afonso de Albuquerque seized the spice-trade hub of Goa, founding Portugal's Asian empire.
body:
Goa became the capital of Portuguese India and a crucial hub for the spice trade. The Portuguese held it for over four centuries with a tiny garrison — a sign of how asymmetric colonial power could be, resting on naval superiority rather than numbers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_conquest_of_Goa).

name: Bartolomé de las Casas advocates for Indigenous peoples
summary: A Spanish Dominican friar documented the atrocities of conquest and argued that Indigenous people were fully human and must not be enslaved.
body:
Las Casas spent forty years in the Americas, witnessed the [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) and brutality of [Spanish conquest](event:spanish-conquest), and wrote *A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies* — a searing indictment that reached the Spanish Crown.

His advocacy did not stop slavery or conquest, but it introduced the principle that colonised peoples had rights that could not be violated — an idea that would echo through the centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas).

name: Protestant Reformation
summary: Western Christianity split, and with it the political order of Europe.
body:
Luther's [Ninety-five Theses](event:95-theses) were carried across Germany by the [printing press](event:printing-press) within weeks. Calvin, Zwingli and Henry VIII produced further breaks; the Catholic Church answered with the Council of Trent.

A century of religious war followed, culminating in the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war) and the [Peace of Westphalia](event:westphalia), which established the sovereign state as the basic unit of European politics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation).

name: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: An Augustinian friar's objections to the sale of indulgences, addressed to his archbishop, became the spark of the Reformation.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). An Augustinian friar's objections to the sale of indulgences, addressed to his archbishop, became the spark of the Reformation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses).

name: First circumnavigation of the globe
summary: Magellan's expedition sailed west around South America and across the Pacific; one ship of five returned under Elcano.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Magellan himself was killed in the Philippines. The survivors proved the world was navigable in one continuous ocean — and discovered they had lost a day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_expedition).

name: Spanish conquest of the Americas
summary: Small Spanish forces, allied with rival Indigenous states and aided by epidemics, overthrew the Aztec and Inca empires.
body:
[Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan) fell in 1521 and [Cusco](event:inca-conquest) in 1533. Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas then financed Habsburg Spain and flowed on to China.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas).

name: Epidemics devastate the Americas
summary: Smallpox, measles and typhus killed an estimated 80–95% of the Indigenous population of the Americas.
body:
Part of [The Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange). Populations with no prior exposure collapsed within decades, often ahead of the Europeans themselves. The depopulation was so vast that regrowing forests may have measurably lowered global CO2 in the early 1600s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas).

name: Suleiman the Magnificent
summary: Under Suleiman, the Ottoman Empire reached its height, stretching from North Africa to the Persian Gulf and up into Hungary.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). Suleiman was called *Kanuni*, the Lawgiver, for codifying Ottoman law; his court at Constantinople was arguably the era's most splendid. The empire controlled the eastern Mediterranean trade, the Silk Road, and the hajj pilgrimage routes.

After his death, the Ottomans became gradually weaker, but remained a great power until 1918.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent).

name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: After a 93-day siege, Cortés and tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies destroyed the Aztec capital.
body:
Part of [Spanish conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest). After a 93-day siege, Cortés and tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies destroyed the Aztec capital.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Tenochtitlan).

name: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: Some 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic in chains; nearly two million died on the voyage.
body:
The trade supplied labour for sugar, tobacco and cotton plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America, and enriched ports from Lisbon to Liverpool. It depopulated regions of West and Central Africa and built the racial hierarchies of the modern Atlantic world.

Britain abolished the trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833; Brazil, the largest importer, abolished slavery only in 1888. See also the [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade).

name: Mughal Empire
summary: Babur's descendants ruled most of the Indian subcontinent, at their height the richest state in the world.
body:
Akbar's religious tolerance and administrative reforms, and the architecture of Shah Jahan including the [Taj Mahal](event:taj-mahal), mark the empire's high point; the [British East India Company](event:british-raj) picked over its decline.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire).

name: Ethiopian–Adal War
summary: The Christian Ethiopian empire and the Muslim Sultanate of Adal fought a devastating war, with Ottoman and Portuguese intervention on opposing sides.
body:
Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi of Adal invaded the Ethiopian highlands in 1529 and overran much of the empire, aided by Ottoman firearms and troops. Ethiopia appealed to Portugal, which landed a musketeer force in 1541; Ahmad was killed at the Battle of Wayna Daga in 1543 and the invasion collapsed.

The war left both states exhausted and the highlands depopulated, but the Ethiopian monarchy and its Orthodox church survived. The Ottomans held only the Red Sea coast, and Ethiopia remained independent.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian%E2%80%93Adal_War).

name: Conquest of the Inca Empire
summary: Pizarro seized the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, took a room full of gold as ransom, and executed him anyway.
body:
Part of [Spanish conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest). Pizarro seized the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, took a room full of gold as ransom, and executed him anyway.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire).

name: Henry VIII breaks with Rome
summary: England's king rejected papal authority, dissolved the monasteries and made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). Henry wanted a son, the Pope would not annul his marriage, so Henry seized church lands and declared himself the final authority on doctrine. The Break with Rome was less about theology than power — Henry remained Catholic in belief — but it pulled England out of Christendom's common orbit.

The confiscated monastic wealth enriched the Tudor state and a new aristocracy, reshaping English society and politics for centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Break_with_Rome).

name: The Scientific Revolution
summary: Europeans replaced inherited authority with mathematics and experiment as the test of what is true about nature.
body:
It runs from [Copernicus](event:copernicus) and Vesalius through [Galileo](event:galileo), Kepler, Bacon and Descartes to [Newton's *Principia*](event:newton) — after which the same laws were known to govern falling apples and orbiting planets.

The habit of publishing, checking and repeating results is arguably the revolution's most durable product.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution).

name: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
summary: *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* argued that the Earth orbits the Sun, published as its author lay dying.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Displacing the Earth from the centre of the cosmos was the first of the great demotions of humanity's cosmic status.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus).

name: Silver boom at Potosí
summary: The silver mountain of Potosí in Upper Peru (modern Bolivia) produced a large share of the world's silver, reshaping global trade at an enormous human cost.
body:
Between 1545 and 1810 Potosí produced roughly two-fifths of the world's silver. The bullion flowed to Spain, financed its wars, and from there into Amsterdam, Venice and the Asian trade — Potosí silver was one of the first genuinely global currencies.

The human cost was severe. Indigenous communities supplied conscripted labour through the Spanish *mita* system, and enslaved Africans were brought in as well; accidents, cave-ins and mercury poisoning from the refining process killed large numbers of workers, though historians' estimates of the total vary widely.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD).

name: Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic Church defined its doctrine against Protestantism and reformed clerical discipline.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The Catholic Church defined its doctrine against Protestantism and reformed clerical discipline.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Trent).

name: Peace of Augsburg
summary: Catholic and Protestant princes agreed to stop fighting over Germany; cuius regio, eius religio — the ruler chooses the faith.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The Peace of Augsburg ended religious civil war in the Holy Roman Empire by letting each territory's prince decide whether his subjects would be Catholic or Lutheran — a revolutionary concession to pluralism, even if it meant forced exile for religious minorities.

The principle held until the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war) shattered it again.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Augsburg).

name: Akbar the Great reigns
summary: Akbar expanded the Mughal Empire across most of the Indian subcontinent and reformed its administration with remarkable tolerance.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). Akbar was illiterate but intellectually voracious; he abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, married a Hindu princess and included Hindus in his administration. His court at Agra became a centre of art and learning, where Hindu and Islamic cultures blended.

His reign established the pattern of Mughal grandeur — seen later in the [Taj Mahal](event:taj-mahal) — and a model of imperial pluralism rarely matched in its era.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar).

name: Manila Galleon trade route
summary: Spanish ships carried Chinese silk and porcelain across the Pacific to Mexico, exchanging them for American silver.
body:
The galleons sailed once a year from Manila to Acapulco, carrying goods worth fortunes, and returned laden with silver from [Potosí](event:potosi-silver) and Mexico. Chinese merchants were the true beneficiaries — they controlled the production of silk and ceramics — but Spain took its cut and Mexico became the Pacific gateway to the Atlantic world.

For two and a half centuries, the Manila Galleon was one of the world's most valuable trade routes, linking three continents through Spanish empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_galleon).

name: Dutch Revolt against Spain
summary: The Low Countries rebelled against Spanish rule, fought a gruelling eighty-year war, and emerged as an independent republic and a global power.
body:
What began as resistance to Spanish taxes and Catholic oppression became a foundational moment for Dutch identity and republican government. The Dutch proved that a wealthy merchant republic could defeat an empire — though not for eighty years of bloodshed.

The independence was sealed at the [Peace of Westphalia](event:westphalia) in 1648, and the Dutch promptly became the world's greatest trading power, rivalling the English and Portuguese in every ocean.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years%27_War).

name: Battle of Lepanto
summary: A Holy League fleet destroyed the Ottoman navy in the last great battle fought mainly by oared galleys.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). A Holy League fleet destroyed the Ottoman navy in the last great battle fought mainly by oared galleys.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lepanto).

name: Defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II's invasion fleet was scattered by English fireships and Atlantic storms.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). Philip II's invasion fleet was scattered by English fireships and Atlantic storms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada).

name: Shakespeare's plays
summary: Thirty-seven plays written for a London commercial theatre became the central works of English literature.
body:
Thirty-seven plays written for a London commercial theatre became the central works of English literature.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare).

name: Edict of Nantes
summary: Henry IV of France granted religious toleration to Huguenots (French Protestants), ending decades of civil war.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The Edict granted Huguenots the right to worship in designated places and promised equality before the law — a rare concession in an age of religious conformity enforced by the sword.

The Edict lasted until Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, driving hundreds of thousands of Huguenots into exile and demonstrating how fragile religious liberty remained.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Nantes).

name: English East India Company founded
summary: Elizabeth I chartered a joint-stock company to trade with Asia; it would become the instrument of British empire in India.
body:
The East India Company started as a trading venture but evolved into a quasi-government, issuing its own currency, maintaining armies, making treaties and collecting taxes. It discovered that political control was necessary for stable trade — so it conquered India piecemeal, justified by commerce.

By 1800 the Company governed Bengal outright and dominated much of the coast, a private corporation exercising sovereign power under a distant Crown.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company).

name: Dutch East India Company founded
summary: The Dutch chartered the VOC, history's first multinational corporation, to dominate the spice trade and later global commerce.
body:
The VOC (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) combined dozens of trading companies into one, backed by the state and stockholders who expected profits. It pursued monopoly by force: to control the nutmeg trade the VOC seized the Banda Islands in 1621, killing or deporting almost the whole Bandanese population.

At its height in the 1700s, the VOC was wealthier than most nations. It proved that commerce, backed by force, could reshape the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company).

name: Tokugawa Japan and sakoku
summary: The Tokugawa shogunate imposed two and a half centuries of internal peace and near-total isolation from the outside world.
body:
Foreign trade was restricted to a single Dutch outpost at Nagasaki until American gunboats forced the country open, precipitating the [Meiji Restoration](event:meiji).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_period).

name: Jamestown settlement
summary: The first permanent English settlement in North America, Jamestown survived disease, famine and Indigenous resistance to anchor English colonization.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). The early years were nightmarish — half the colonists died in the first year — but tobacco cultivation made profit possible. Indentured servants and then enslaved Africans provided the labour; the Powhatan Confederacy resisted but was gradually driven back.

Jamestown became Virginia, which became a cornerstone of English North America and, eventually, the United States.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown,_Virginia).

name: Founding of Quebec
summary: Samuel de Champlain established the first permanent French settlement in North America, centred on the fur trade and alliance with Algonquian peoples.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Unlike [Jamestown](event:jamestown), Quebec succeeded through partnership with Indigenous nations rather than conquest — the French needed Indigenous hunters to supply furs. This created a different colonial path, with more intermarriage and métis (mixed-race) populations.

Quebec became the capital of New France and the foundation of Francophone North America.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_City#Colonial_era).

name: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
summary: Planets move in ellipses, sweeping equal areas in equal times — the first mathematically exact astronomy.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Planets move in ellipses, sweeping equal areas in equal times — the first mathematically exact astronomy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion).

name: Galileo turns a telescope on the sky
summary: Moons around Jupiter, phases of Venus and mountains on the Moon: the heavens were neither perfect nor Earth-centred.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). His advocacy of [Copernicus](event:copernicus) brought him before the Inquisition in 1633 and house arrest for the rest of his life.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_Galilei).

name: Thirty Years' War
summary: A religious quarrel in Bohemia became a general European war that killed perhaps a third of the German population.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). A religious quarrel in Bohemia became a general European war that killed perhaps a third of the German population.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War).

name: Harvey discovers blood circulation
summary: William Harvey proved that blood circulates through the body, pumped by the heart — overturning medicine's ancient consensus in one blow.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Harvey used mathematics and dissection to prove that the blood flows in a loop, not ebbing and flowing as Galen had taught for 1,500 years. His *De motu cordis* was published while he was physician to Charles I, and he was 50 when it appeared.

The discovery opened a new physiology and was the foundation on which cardiovascular medicine was built.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey).

name: Taj Mahal built
summary: Shah Jahan built a white marble mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal on the Yamuna.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). Shah Jahan built a white marble mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal on the Yamuna.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal).

name: English Civil War
summary: Parliament defeated and then executed Charles I, the first European monarch tried and beheaded by his own subjects.
body:
Parliament defeated and then executed Charles I, the first European monarch tried and beheaded by his own subjects.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War).

name: Qing dynasty
summary: Manchu rulers conquered Ming China and expanded it to its greatest territorial extent, before collapsing under internal revolt and foreign pressure.
body:
The [Taiping Rebellion](event:taiping) and the [Opium Wars](event:opium-wars) hollowed out the dynasty; it fell in 1912.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty).

name: Peace of Westphalia
summary: The treaties ended the war and are conventionally taken to establish the modern system of sovereign states.
body:
Part of [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). The treaties ended the war and are conventionally taken to establish the modern system of sovereign states.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia).

name: Aurangzeb expands the Mughal Empire
summary: The last great Mughal emperor conquered southern India but alienated Hindus with religious orthodoxy, sowing the empire's decline.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). Aurangzeb reversed [Akbar](event:akbar-great)'s tolerance, imposed Islamic law strictly and taxed Hindus discriminatorily. His long southern wars enriched the treasury but exhausted it too — by his death the empire was stretched thin.

Without his military genius to hold it together, the Mughal state fragmented into provincial kingdoms that the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) could divide and conquer.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb).

name: Kangxi Emperor consolidates Qing Dynasty
summary: Kangxi extended Qing rule over Mongolia, Taiwan and Tibet, and presided over a cultural and economic golden age.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). Kangxi was a scholar-emperor who loved poetry, calligraphy and scholarship. He toured his realm extensively, showed concern for the welfare of the common people, and filled his court with able administrators.

Under his rule, China was peaceful and prosperous, the empire expanded steadily on its northern and western frontiers, and the population grew rapidly. He died leaving the dynasty at its height.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangxi_Emperor).

name: Boyle's law of gases
summary: Robert Boyle showed that gas pressure and volume are inversely related, laying the foundation of chemistry and thermodynamics.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Boyle's law — pressure times volume is constant — was the first mathematical law governing the behaviour of matter itself, and it proved that gases obeyed the same natural laws as solids and liquids.

It was among the first triumphs of the experimental method and helped establish chemistry as a quantitative science.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle%27s_law).

name: Robert Hooke discovers cells
summary: Using an early microscope, Hooke observed the cellular structure of cork and coined the term 'cell' to describe life's basic unit.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Hooke's *Micrographia* (1665) was one of the era's most beautifully illustrated books, with detailed drawings of microscopic organisms and structures. He saw honeycomb-like compartments in plant tissue and called them 'cells', not realizing he had glimpsed the basis of all life.

Cell biology would not mature for another two centuries, but Hooke had found the door.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hooke).

name: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes reveal microorganisms
summary: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground tiny lenses to magnify water droplets 200-fold and discovered bacteria, protozoa and blood cells.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Leeuwenhoek was an obsessive lens-grinder, not a university man, but his hand-built microscopes surpassed all competitors. He saw what nobody else had imagined — a teeming world of life in a drop of water.

He spent decades describing what he saw, in hundreds of letters to the Royal Society, proving that life extended far below the threshold of the naked eye.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek).

name: Christopher Wren builds St. Paul's Cathedral
summary: After the Great Fire of 1666 burned old London, Wren designed a new baroque cathedral that became the architectural symbol of a restored Britain.
body:
St. Paul's took 35 years to build and consumed vast resources during [the Glorious Revolution](event:glorious-revolution) and the wars with Louis XIV. Wren's soaring dome became the image of London, rising again from ashes, reassuring and grand.

Wren designed over 50 churches after the fire and pioneered English baroque — a style less florid than the Continental version, more restrained and mathematical.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul%27s_Cathedral).

name: Peter the Great modernizes Russia
summary: Peter I dragged Russia into the modern world by force, building a navy, westernising the court and making Russia a European great power.
body:
Peter visited Western Europe incognito to study shipbuilding and returned to Russia determined to transform it. He cut off the nobles' beards, reformed the alphabet, moved the capital to [St. Petersburg](event:st-petersburg-founded) on the Baltic, and fought Sweden for access to the sea.

He was brutal — crushing a rebellion of the old guard with public executions — but he succeeded in making Russia a force to reckon with in European politics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great).

name: Ottoman siege of Vienna
summary: A Polish-led relief army broke the siege, marking the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion in Europe.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). A Polish-led relief army broke the siege, marking the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion in Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vienna).

name: J.S. Bach's compositions
summary: Johann Sebastian Bach composed some of humanity's greatest music — mathematically intricate fugues and spiritually profound works for the church.
body:
Bach worked in provincial German courts and churches, never travelled far, and was not famous in his own time. He composed over 1,000 pieces: suites, concertos, cantatas and the *Art of Fugue*, in which counterpoint becomes almost a philosophy of order.

After his death his work fell into obscurity until the 19th-century revival that made him a titan. He is now considered the summit of baroque music.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach).

name: The Enlightenment
summary: European thinkers argued that reason, evidence and individual rights, not tradition or revelation, should organise society.
body:
Locke, Voltaire, Hume, Rousseau, Kant, Smith and Diderot were read across a continent-wide republic of letters. Their arguments underwrote the [American](event:american-revolution) and [French](event:french-revolution) revolutions, the abolition of the [slave trade](event:slave-trade), and the idea of progress itself.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment).

name: Newton's Principia
summary: Three laws of motion and universal gravitation explained falling bodies, tides, comets and planetary orbits with one system.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Newton also invented calculus to do it. The *Principia* is arguably the most influential scientific book ever written, and it made physics the model to which every other science aspired for two hundred years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophiæ_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica).

name: Glorious Revolution
summary: Parliament invited William of Orange to replace James II, and attached a Bill of Rights to the crown.
body:
Constitutional monarchy, parliamentary supremacy and the Bank of England follow from this settlement.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution).

name: Voltaire's philosophy and writings
summary: Voltaire attacked superstition, censorship and religious intolerance with satire and reason, becoming the voice of the Enlightenment.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Voltaire lived a long, scandalous and prolific life — writing poetry, philosophy, history and *Candide*, a dark satire on optimism that remains funny and bitter today. He was imprisoned for insulting the powerful and exiled, but his ideas spread across Europe through letters and smuggled books.

He died in Paris celebrated as the greatest living writer, his pen having sharpened the weapons of reason against the Old Regime.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire).

name: Founding of St. Petersburg
summary: Peter the Great built a new capital on the Baltic marshes to give Russia a window on Europe and shake off Moscow's old ways.
body:
Part of [Peter the Great](event:peter-the-great)'s modernisation. St. Petersburg was built in a European style with straight streets and grand buildings, and was intended to rival Western cities in culture and sophistication. Thousands of workers died in the swamps; the city cost a vast sum.

But it succeeded. St. Petersburg became Russia's window on the West and remained the capital until 1918.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg).

name: Act of Union creates Great Britain
summary: The parliaments of England and Scotland merged, turning a shared monarchy into a single kingdom of Great Britain.
body:
The two crowns had shared a monarch since 1603; the 1707 Acts joined the parliaments as well. The Union was partly economic (Scotland gained access to English colonial markets), partly religious (both were Protestant) and partly practical — one monarch, one parliament, one army and navy could project power farther than two squabbling realms.

The union held the British Isles together for colonial conquest and, as Britain, made it the world's greatest imperial power by 1800.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707).

name: Yongzheng Emperor's Qing reforms
summary: Yongzheng tightened imperial authority, reformed the bureaucracy and reduced corruption, strengthening the Qing state.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). Yongzheng succeeded his father [Kangxi](event:kangxi-emperor) and proved an even more meticulous administrator. He created a secret memorial system to bypass bureaucratic channels, settled border disputes, and boosted agricultural productivity.

His reign was short but crucial in stabilising Qing power, setting the stage for his successors to govern a stable empire of 300 million people.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongzheng_Emperor).

name: Hume's empiricist philosophy
summary: David Hume argued that all knowledge comes from experience, not reason or revelation, shaking the foundations of metaphysics.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Hume published his *Treatise of Human Nature* in 1739 and spent the rest of his life elaborating and defending empiricism — the view that the senses, not pure reason, are the source of knowledge.

He argued we cannot prove God, causation or the self — only experience impressions. His radical scepticism troubled philosophers then and now, but it steered thought toward experimental science.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume).

name: Enlightened despotism in Prussia and Austria
summary: Absolute monarchs like Frederick the Great and Maria Theresa adopted Enlightenment reforms — legal codes, religious toleration, education — while keeping power.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). 'Everything for the people, nothing by the people' is the phrase later used to sum up the approach. Frederick the Great reformed the law, promoted science, and invited philosophers like Voltaire to his court.

Enlightened despotism showed that Enlightenment ideas could be imposed from above, even if they contradicted monarchy itself — a tension that would break open in the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism).

name: Montesquieu's separation of powers
summary: Montesquieu argued that liberty depends on dividing government into legislative, executive and judicial branches.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). *The Spirit of the Laws* was widely read and directly influenced the design of the [American Constitution](event:us-constitution). The idea that separated powers check each other remains the template for democratic design.

Montesquieu also believed different climates and conditions shaped different forms of government — an early comparative politics that was partly prejudiced but also insightful.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu).

name: Diderot's Encyclopédie
summary: Denis Diderot edited a massive encyclopedia of human knowledge — 28 volumes — that was both radical philosophy and a technical handbook.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). The *Encyclopédie* covered everything: philosophy, trades, politics, science, carpentry, music. It was collaborative, featuring contributions from [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social) and others, and was constantly harassed by the authorities for subversion.

By distributing knowledge widely, it embodied Enlightenment faith that reason and facts would reform society.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopédie).

name: Konbaung Dynasty unites Burma
summary: Alaungpaya and his Konbaung successors reunified Burma after fragmentation, created a powerful kingdom and resisted European control.
body:
Burma had been divided and weak; Alaungpaya's military genius reconquered the country and invaded Siam; his successors later fought off four Qing invasions. His successors expanded Burmese power to its greatest extent, controlling a territory from the Andaman Sea to the Assamese hills.

The British would conquer Burma in three wars by 1885, but the Konbaung had created a Burmese nation-state where there had been scattered kingdoms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konbaung_Dynasty).

name: Lisbon earthquake
summary: An earthquake, tsunami and fire destroyed one of Europe's great capitals on All Saints' Day.
body:
Tens of thousands died. The disaster shook Enlightenment optimism — Voltaire's *Candide* is a direct response — and prompted the first systematic scientific survey of an earthquake.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake).

name: Mozart's compositions
summary: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed over 600 works across every genre of the Classical era, dying at 35 having transformed European music.
body:
Mozart was a prodigy who was touring Europe by age six and wrote his first symphony at eight. His mature works — the late symphonies, the great operas, the piano concertos — combine mathematical precision with emotional depth.

He died poor and was buried in a pauper's grave, but his music outlived all the princes and bishops he served.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart).

name: Seven Years' War
summary: A war fought in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines — arguably the first global conflict.
body:
Britain took Canada and effective control of Bengal; the debts it ran up led it to tax the American colonies, with consequences it did not expect.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years%27_War).

name: Battle of Plassey
summary: Robert Clive's East India Company army defeated the Nawab of Bengal in a single afternoon, beginning the British conquest of India.
body:
Clive's [East India Company](event:english-east-india) force of about 3,000 faced perhaps 50,000, but he had disciplined artillery and a downpour that spoiled the Nawab's powder. The victory was above all political: Clive had already bought off Mir Jafar, the Nawab's own commander, who held the bulk of the army out of the fight and took the throne afterwards.

Plassey opened Bengal to the Company, which took over the province's revenues in 1765 and expanded across much of the subcontinent over the following decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey).

name: Industrial Revolution
summary: Machines powered by coal replaced muscle, and for the first time in history sustained economic growth outran population growth.
body:
It began with textiles and [steam](event:watt-engine) in Britain, spread to iron, chemicals and [railways](event:railways), and within a century had remade work, cities, class and warfare.

Human living standards, life expectancy and energy use all bend sharply upward from this point — as does atmospheric CO2, the beginning of [modern climate change](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution).

name: Rousseau's The Social Contract
summary: Rousseau argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed expressed through the 'general will'.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Where [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment) attacked religion, Rousseau attacked society itself as corrupting humans' natural goodness. His *Social Contract* provided arguments for democracy and was seized by both the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) and by authoritarian regimes who claimed to embody the 'general will'.

His ideas remain fertile and dangerous, read by revolutionaries and conservatives alike.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Social_Contract).

name: Mechanised spinning
summary: Hargreaves' spinning jenny and Arkwright's water frame multiplied the output of a single worker many times over.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). Hargreaves' spinning jenny and Arkwright's water frame multiplied the output of a single worker many times over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny).

name: Goethe's literary influence
summary: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was Germany's greatest writer, whose works bridged the Enlightenment and Romanticism.
body:
*The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) was the first international bestseller, making Goethe famous before he was 25. His poetry, plays and novels moved beyond Enlightenment rationality toward emotion and the power of nature.

By 1800, Goethe had become Germany's intellectual leader, influential across Europe and a model for the Romantic movement that followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wolfgang_von_Goethe).

name: American Revolution
summary: Thirteen British colonies declared themselves independent and, with French help, made it stick.
body:
The [Declaration of Independence](event:declaration-independence) asserted that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed; victory at [Yorktown](event:yorktown) secured it, and the [Constitution](event:us-constitution) of 1787 turned it into a working federal republic.

The example — and the debts France ran up supporting it — helped bring on the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution).

name: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
summary: The founding text of economics argued that specialisation and free exchange, not hoarded bullion, create national wealth.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). The founding text of economics argued that specialisation and free exchange, not hoarded bullion, create national wealth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations).

name: Watt's steam engine
summary: A separate condenser made the steam engine efficient enough to power factories anywhere, not just to pump out mines.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). A separate condenser made the steam engine efficient enough to power factories anywhere, not just to pump out mines.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine).

name: Declaration of Independence
summary: The Continental Congress adopted Jefferson's declaration that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). The Continental Congress adopted Jefferson's declaration that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence).

name: Tay Son Rebellion in Vietnam
summary: Rural rebels in southern Vietnam overthrew the aristocracy, briefly unified the country and redistributed land before being crushed.
body:
The Tay Son were peasants who rebelled against both the Nguyen lords of the south and the Trinh lords of the north, winning astonishing victories despite being outnumbered. They redistributed confiscated aristocratic lands to the poor and proclaimed a meritocracy.

They routed a Qing invasion in 1789, but after their leader Nguyen Hue died in 1792 the movement fractured, and Nguyen Anh — backed by French advisers — reconquered the country by 1802 — though the Tay Son legacy of peasant revolt echoed into the 20th century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tây_Sơn_dynasty).

name: Siege of Yorktown
summary: A Franco-American army and a French fleet trapped Cornwallis, effectively ending the war.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). A Franco-American army and a French fleet trapped Cornwallis, effectively ending the war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown).

name: Chakri Dynasty founded in Siam
summary: General Chakri founded a new royal house in Siam (Thailand) that rules to this day, making it the world's longest-reigning monarchy.
body:
After the Burmese destroyed the previous Siamese capital at Ayutthaya, Chakri established a new one at Bangkok and created a stable, centralised state. Siam remained independent through both British and French colonialism, a feat achieved by careful diplomacy and strategic modernisation.

The Chakri dynasty still reigns, having survived wars, revolutions and coups for over 240 years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakri_Dynasty).

name: United States Constitution
summary: A written constitution with separated powers, federalism and (from 1791) a Bill of Rights.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). It is the oldest national constitution still in force, and the model for most written constitutions since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States).

name: French Revolution
summary: The old European order of monarchy, aristocracy and established church was overthrown in its most powerful state.
body:
From the storming of the [Bastille](event:bastille) and the [Declaration of the Rights of Man](event:rights-of-man) through the [Terror](event:terror) to [Napoleon's coup](event:napoleon-coup), the revolution ran through every political possibility in ten years.

It exported the vocabulary of modern politics — left and right, nation, citizen, ideology — and its wars remade Europe as the [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution).

name: Storming of the Bastille
summary: A Paris crowd took the royal fortress-prison on 14 July, still France's national day.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). A Paris crowd took the royal fortress-prison on 14 July, still France's national day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille).

name: Declaration of the Rights of Man
summary: Liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression declared the natural rights of every man.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). Liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression declared the natural rights of every man.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_the_Rights_of_Man_and_of_the_Citizen).

name: Haitian Revolution
summary: Enslaved people in France's richest colony overthrew their masters and founded the first Black republic.
body:
Toussaint Louverture's army defeated French, Spanish and British forces. It is the only successful large-scale slave revolt in modern history, and it terrified slaveholding societies everywhere — see the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Revolution).

name: The Reign of Terror
summary: The Committee of Public Safety executed some 17,000 people, including the king, the queen and finally Robespierre.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). The Committee of Public Safety executed some 17,000 people, including the king, the queen and finally Robespierre.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Terror).

name: Jenner's smallpox vaccine
summary: Edward Jenner showed that cowpox inoculation protects against smallpox, founding vaccination.
body:
The technique eventually [eradicated smallpox](event:smallpox-eradication) — the only human disease ever deliberately wiped out.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine).

name: Napoleon seizes power
summary: The coup of 18 Brumaire ended the Directory and made Bonaparte First Consul; he crowned himself emperor in 1804.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). The coup of 18 Brumaire ended the Directory and made Bonaparte First Consul; he crowned himself emperor in 1804.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_of_18_Brumaire).
